days.title: Murray Bowen (*Reading the Pattern Between People, Triangles & Overfunctioning*)

cards.label: Core Idea
cards.title: Part 1 — Murray Bowen (*Reading the Pattern Between People, Triangles & Overfunctioning*)
cards.md:
**Thesis Opener:** In `Bk1`–`Bk3` you read the room's culture, brokered across tribes, and steadied your bridge self; in `Bk4` you step up to **systemic steering**—reading the live emotional circuit running *between* people and changing your own role in it without blaming whoever appears to be driving it.

Picture a room not as a collection of isolated personalities, but as an **emotional circuit** where tension moves along predictable pathways. **Murray Bowen's** family and emotional systems theory maps the core recurring circuits groups use to manage anxiety: **conflict**, **distance**, **emotional cut-off**, **overfunctioning/underfunctioning reciprocity**, and **triangles**. Whenever tension rises between two people, an automatic reflex pulls in a third person or issue to offload the anxiety—forming a **triangle** (in teams, two colleagues bonding by complaining about a third; in families, venting sideways instead of speaking directly). Similarly, **overfunctioning** (taking over, rescuing, over-explaining) and **underfunctioning** (going passive, waiting to be carried) lock together as a reciprocal seesaw: the harder one person pushes to compensate, the further the other steps back. Because a system reacts automatically whenever one member changes their habitual role, the leverage point is never fixing or lecturing the others—it is **modifying your own part in the circuit** while staying in calm, non-polarized contact.
*Bridge to Tuesday:* Bowen shows how to spot the circuit and step out of your habitual slot; tomorrow, **Bill Torbert** gives you the linguistic move to name that pattern aloud and shift what the conversation is actually about.

cards.label: In Action
cards.title: Part 1 — Murray Bowen (*Reading the Pattern Between People, Triangles & Overfunctioning*)
cards.md:
- **Operational Bridge:** Before speaking into group friction, check whether you are being pulled into a **triangle** or an **overfunctioning** reflex—and alter your own move first rather than trying to police the room.
- **Office Worked Example:** When a teammate vents privately about a third colleague's missed handoff instead of raising it directly, refuse to carry the complaint: *“I hear that the delay put pressure on your timeline—have you checked in with them directly on what's blocking it?”*
- **Personal Worked Example:** When a group or family routine stalls and your reflex is to overfunction (planning everything, smoothing every awkward pause), hold back one notch and let others step into the space.
- **Non-Example:** Stepping into a tense two-person disagreement to mediate uninvited or lecturing someone on how *“triangulated”* they are being.
- **Decision Rule & Handoff:** Change your own automatic move in the circuit before proposing a group reframe. Feeds your `Bk4` pattern diagnosis and systemic steering plan.

cards.md:
### Layer 3 · Optional Deepening (Susanne Cook-Greuter — *9 Levels of Ego Development* & Strategist Self-Inclusion)

Cook-Greuter notes that systems-level meaning-making recognizes circular, tapestry-like influences—and includes **one's own meaning-making as a node inside the system**. The subtle shadow at this level is **the transformer's loop**: seeing everything in the system except the part of yourself that needs to be the helper or fixer.

days.label: Tuesday
days.title: Bill Torbert (*Double-Loop Learning, Naming the Dynamic & Reframing on Purpose*)

cards.label: Core Idea
cards.title: Part 2 — Bill Torbert (*Double-Loop Learning, Naming the Dynamic & Reframing on Purpose*)
cards.md:
**Thesis Opener:** Monday mapped the invisible circuit running between people; **Bill Torbert** moves from silent observation to **double-loop systemic steering**—naming the pattern tentatively without blame and proposing a frame that changes what the conversation is actually about.

Think of organizational and interpersonal learning across three concentric loops. **Single-loop learning** adjusts tactics to hit an existing goal more efficiently; **double-loop learning** steps back to question the goal, frame, or underlying assumptions themselves; and **triple-loop awareness** attends in real time to the quality of attention doing the questioning.
When a meeting or relationship slides into a zero-sum tug-of-war, arguing harder inside the old frame is single-loop friction. Systemic steering is a **double-loop move**: you **attack the pattern, not the person**, name the dynamic **tentatively** with an invitation to correct you (*“I notice we're treating this like a status fight, when it might actually be a resource constraint—does that match how you're seeing it?”*), and offer a cleaner frame (*“Let's treat this as a design problem rather than a debate”*). Once you propose the frame, **seal it with your own pace, tone, and posture** from Brown Belt so your analogic delivery matches your words.
*Bridge to Wednesday:* Naming and reframing can shift a stuck room rapidly—which makes **timing and readiness** the decisive guardrail on Wednesday.

### Layer 3 · Optional Deepening (Robert Kegan — Malleable Metaphors & *In Over Our Heads*)

Kegan compares well-offered reframes to **soft clay rather than cold analysis**: when a frame is offered tentatively in language the room can touch and reshape, people engage with it as co-authors rather than resisting an external diagnosis.

days.label: Wednesday
days.title: Room Readiness & The Strategist's Blind Spot (*Naming Only What the Room Can Hold*)

cards.label: Core Idea
cards.title: Part 3 — Room Readiness & The Strategist's Blind Spot (*Naming Only What the Room Can Hold*)
cards.md:
**Thesis Opener:** Monday and Tuesday gave you the lens to see the circuit and the words to reframe it; **Wednesday** installs the essential brake—**calibrating for readiness** so your insight lands as clarity rather than overwhelm or condescension.

Picture a bridge engineer testing how much load a span can safely carry before rolling heavy equipment across it. **Bill Torbert** flags a signature blind spot of systems-level thinkers: **overestimating others' readiness** for a full systemic diagnosis. Seeing a pattern clearly does not mean the room is ready—or asking—to hear the whole map at once.
When you name three layers of hidden dynamics to a room that is still trying to solve a concrete task, two things happen: people feel analyzed rather than met, and the conversation stalls in confusion or defensiveness. **Light naming that lands** beats a comprehensive diagnosis that triggers resistance. Hearing the person *before* naming the pattern—and asking *“What matters most here? What am I missing?”* before synthesizing—keeps systemic steering grounded in genuine mutuality rather than intellectual performance.
*Bridge to Thursday & Friday:* You now hold all three `Bk4` lenses—Bowen's system circuits, Torbert's tentative double-loop reframing, and readiness calibration. Test them in Thursday's **Systemic Steering Lab** and complete Friday's `Bk4` deliverable.

cards.label: In Action
cards.title: Part 3 — Room Readiness & The Strategist's Blind Spot (*Naming Only What the Room Can Hold*)
cards.md:
- **Operational Bridge:** Match the depth of your reframe to what the room can actually use right now—acknowledge people's immediate concern first, name one clear dynamic lightly, and land one practical next step.
- **Office Worked Example:** Instead of unpacking a team's entire cross-departmental history in a 30-minute sprint check, acknowledge the deadline pressure first and offer one clean structural shift: *“It sounds like both teams are protecting quality—let's agree on one shared handoff checklist before Friday.”*
- **Personal Worked Example:** When a friend is venting about a recurring pattern, listen and validate their experience first rather than jumping immediately to *“Here's the systemic cycle you're in.”*
- **Non-Example:** Reframing someone's immediate pain as *“a valuable developmental polarity”* before they feel heard.
- **Decision Rule & Handoff:** Hear the person before the pattern, name only as much of the dynamic as the room can hold, and close every reframe with a concrete action. Completes `Bk4` and sets up `Bk5` (*Systemic Guarding*).

cards.label: Go Deeper
cards.title: Part 3 — Room Readiness & The Strategist's Blind Spot (*Naming Only What the Room Can Hold*)
cards.md:
### Layer 3 · Optional Deepening (Beginner's Mind Protocol — Strategist Growth Edge)

Before offering any systemic synthesis, run three checks: *(1) What is this like for you? (2) What matters most here? (3) What am I missing?* Letting others' answers reshape your map keeps systems insight alive and honest.

cards.title: Deliberate Practice Lab — Systemic Steering Simulator
cards.md:
## Deliberate Practice Lab — Systemic Steering Simulator

:::note
1. **Bowen Circuit Map:** Diagram one recurring loop at work or home (Triangle or Overfunctioning/Underfunctioning). Write the **exact habitual move** you will stop making first.
2. **Soft-Clay Reframe:** Draft a 2-sentence tentative reframe (`Observable pattern + “I wonder if…” + Concrete 5-minute next step`).
3. **Readiness Trim:** Cut your draft by 50% so it lands cleanly in a busy, low-patience room without sounding clinical.
:::
